issue_context.title: Statistics `_statistics_at_time` query is slow with postgresql version 13.9
issue_context.body:
### The problem

State history is very slow to load for some entities.  It appears to be just those entities with a `state_class`.  Loading state history for the past 24 hours for these entities can easily take 20 - 40 seconds..

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

2022.11.3

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

_No response_

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant Core

### Integration causing the issue

_No response_

### Link to integration documentation on our website

_No response_

### Diagnostics information

_No response_

### Example YAML snippet

_No response_

### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

_No response_

### Additional information

I'm not sure when this started but fairly recently.  I noticed that state history for some entities is now querying and returning statistics data and not just state data, so I believe this issue started whenever this switch occurred.

1.  Why is state history attempting to return statistics data?  This is unexpected and unintuitive to me.  Shouldn't state history only be querying the states table?  If I want statistics I would use one of the statistics cards.

2.  Even though the data is coming from `statistics_short_term`, it's not actually showing any statistics.  Every data point either shows a min / mean / max that are all the same:

![Screen Shot 2022-11-20 at 7 25 58 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/24720046/202904688-81a63cca-ef43-42d2-b65f-f9c5ba1d94a9.png)

OR shows just one of those values:

![Screen Shot 2022-11-20 at 7 26 08 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/24720046/202904709-d2907715-3caa-451c-9187-d5a1c9b2f0af.png)

Here's the query for that graph:

```SQL
SELECT statistics_short_term.metadata_id AS statistics_short_term_metadata_id, statistics_short_term.start AS statistics_short_term_start, statistics_short_term.mean AS statistics_short_term_mean, statistics_short_term.min AS statistics_short_term_min, statistics_short_term.max AS statistics_short_term_max, statistics_short_term.last_reset AS statistics_short_term_last_reset, statistics_short_term.state AS statistics_short_term_state, statistics_short_term.sum AS statistics_short_term_sum 
FROM statistics_short_term JOIN 
(SELECT max(statistics_short_term.id) AS max_id FROM statistics_short_term
WHERE statistics_short_term.start < '2022-11-19T13:27:55.851000+00:00'::timestamptz AND statistics_short_term.metadata_id IN (58) GROUP BY statistics_short_term.metadata_id) 
AS anon_1 ON statistics_short_term.id = anon_1.max_id
```

The EXPLAIN plan:

```SQL
-[ RECORD 1 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN | Nested Loop  (cost=1131.86..74668.67 rows=119 width=60)
-[ RECORD 2 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |   ->  GroupAggregate  (cost=1131.42..73661.93 rows=119 width=8)
-[ RECORD 3 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |         Group Key: statistics_short_term_1.metadata_id
-[ RECORD 4 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |         ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on statistics_short_term statistics_short_term_1  (cost=1131.42..73167.75 rows=98599 width=8)
-[ RECORD 5 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |               Recheck Cond: (metadata_id = 58)
-[ RECORD 6 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |               Filter: (start < '2022-11-19 07:27:55.851-06'::timestamp with time zone)
-[ RECORD 7 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |               ->  Bitmap Index Scan on ix_statistics_short_term_metadata_id  (cost=0.00..1106.77 rows=98979 width=0)
-[ RECORD 8 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |                     Index Cond: (metadata_id = 58)
-[ RECORD 9 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |   ->  Index Scan using statistics_short_term_pkey on statistics_short_term  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=64)
-[ RECORD 10 ]-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
QUERY PLAN |         Index Cond: (id = (max(statistics_short_term_1.id)))
```

Here are the relevant indexes:
```SQL
-[ RECORD 1 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
schemaname | public
tablename  | statistics_short_term
indexname  | statistics_short_term_pkey
tablespace | 
indexdef   | CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statistics_short_term_pkey ON public.statistics_short_term USING btree (id)
-[ RECORD 2 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
schemaname | public
tablename  | statistics_short_term
indexname  | ix_statistics_short_term_metadata_id
tablespace | 
indexdef   | CREATE INDEX ix_statistics_short_term_metadata_id ON public.statistics_short_term USING btree (metadata_id)
-[ RECORD 3 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
schemaname | public
tablename  | statistics_short_term
indexname  | ix_statistics_short_term_start
tablespace | 
indexdef   | CREATE INDEX ix_statistics_short_term_start ON public.statistics_short_term USING btree (start)
-[ RECORD 4 ]--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
schemaname | public
tablename  | statistics_short_term
indexname  | ix_statistics_short_term_statistic_id_start
tablespace | 
indexdef   | CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ix_statistics_short_term_statistic_id_start ON public.statistics_short_term USING btree (metadata_id, start)
```

3. I have over a year's worth of data in my database (Postgres) and ~99k rows in `statistics_short_term` for this sensor.  I can query a month's worth of state data for this sensor in the History tab in about 5 seconds, but viewing state history for the past 24 hours takes 20-40 seconds. It doesn't make sense to me why we're querying `statistics_short_term` to show state data, especially when it's not even showing me any actual statistics.  Assuming I'm not missing an index and that this is intended behavior, can we at least add an option to revert the state history graph to how it was before when it was pulling from the `states` table for all entities?
comments:
Same situation. 1 year database data in postgres. Very slow since changing to statistics graph (20-30 seconds).
If I click "Toon meer", the history data is instant.

Hardware is a 1.8GHz dualcore celeron with 8 Gig ram and 240Gb nvme drive.

I removed everything older than a month in the short term statistics table and now it is very fast.
But this query should be fast with a lot of data and an index.

Agreed.  I still think we should revert to the old style of showing state history, or provide an option to default to either state history or statistics.  However, either way it seems like the statistics table needs a better index.

> Is there an easy way for me to exclude certain entities from the dump such as device tracker location data?

Nope there isn't.  But you could restore it into a new database and replace the state_attributes json values with '{}' via an update query. Than dump that database instead. Unfortunately that may make the data more difficult to examine.
Also if you are worried about sharing recent location data you could always dump it now and wait a week to share it so all the data would be stale.

It doesn't look like an index is missing from your query above.  Your explain above shows the maximum rows to be around 100k transversed in that query so I don't think that is the issue.  I think its optimizing the group by poorly.  But I'd probably have to do quite a bit of trial and error with the data to find a query that optimizes well so its unlikely I'll be successful without the actual data.
